strengths: The paper studies a useful and identifiable problem—contextual combinatorial semi-bandits with changing arm availability—and presents the setting, oracle model, and O’CLOK-UCB algorithm clearly. The complete manuscript was assessed here: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-wqrl8k80/call-11d113bdfba4426b868a8ff2c06bd24b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The proposed use of an availability-restricted information-gain quantity is natural, and accounting for covariance among arms selected simultaneously is a meaningful technical issue. If established rigorously, the high-probability approximation-regret result would interest researchers working on GP and combinatorial bandits.

The sparse-GP variant addresses the severe computational cost of exact GP updates. The experiments examine runtime, inducing-point count, and several levels of arm correlation rather than reporting only a single favorable configuration.
The manuscript is generally well organized, includes proof details, relates the result to adaptive-discretization approaches and recent GP-bandit work, and provides a code link.
weaknesses: Necessary: The main regret theorem is not established by the current proof. In Lemma 1, the selected contexts are treated as deterministic merely because the algorithm and oracle have no internal randomization. In fact, each selection depends on previous noisy observations through the posterior mean. Consequently, the adaptive observation vector is not generally jointly Gaussian in the manner used in equations (16)–(18), and its conditional entropy given the adaptively indexed function values need not equal the sum of independent-noise entropies. A plausible repair is to formulate the information gain for each realized, fixed design and prove the required pathwise inequality using block-determinant/Schur-complement identities, but that argument is absent.

Necessary: Several modeling assumptions conflict with the claimed applications. A nondegenerate GP with additive Gaussian noise produces unbounded real outcomes, whereas the paper assumes nonnegative rewards and treats GP values as probabilities in probabilistic coverage. The matching and synthetic sum rewards can be negative; the logarithmic crowdsourcing reward can be negative or even undefined; and un-clipped UCBs can fall outside the probability domain where coverage is monotone and Lipschitz. The theory or the application claims must be narrowed, or an appropriate link/clipping construction and corresponding analysis must be supplied.

Necessary: The MovieLens experiment uses Bernoulli observations and a hand-specified sigmoid response rather than the Gaussian observation model and GP-sampled function assumed by the theorem. Moreover, its theoretical budget K bounds selected base arms, while the experiment calls three selected movies K even though a super arm contains many movie–user edges. These departures should be stated explicitly and the mapping to the formal model corrected.

Necessary: The empirical language is too strong. Near equality to a randomized approximate TIM+ benchmark does not demonstrate “optimal performance,” and five repetitions across largely synthetic or semi-synthetic outcomes do not by themselves establish broad superiority in realistic settings. Comparisons also lack a documented, comparable hyperparameter-selection protocol.

Necessary: Reproducibility details contain contradictions: Simulation I has 250 rounds but configures CC-MAB using 300; the methods list 10, 20, and 50 inducing points although results include 100; CPU models differ across sections; and the displayed squared-exponential kernel lacks a squared norm. The sparse posterior procedure also needs enough detail to determine whether all observations are retained, how inducing variables are optimized, and whether inducing locations are resampled each round.

Necessary: Other proof conditions require correction or clarification. Equations (1)–(2) omit the allowed nonzero GP prior mean; Lemma 2 assumes fixed context-arrival sets despite broader “arbitrary” availability language; and squaring inequality (22) is invalid without first handling potentially negative approximation regret. These issues are individually repairable but collectively prevent the current theoretical evidence from being fully convincing.

Optional: Stronger evaluation would include sensitivity to kernel misspecification and noise, more trials, tuned baselines, a comparable GP-based baseline, and an explicit empirical/theoretical discussion of the dependence on K and the data-dependent eigenvalue λ*(K).

strengths: The paper addresses a coherent and practically relevant setting combining contextual generalization, combinatorial actions, semi-bandit feedback, and time-varying arm availability. This should interest researchers working on Gaussian-process and combinatorial bandits.

O'CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple, and the main high-probability alpha-approximation regret bound usefully captures changing availability through a restricted information-gain quantity. The treatment of correlated arms selected in batches is a meaningful technical contribution.

The theoretical development is largely self-contained, progressing from simultaneous GP confidence bounds through the approximation-oracle argument to the covariance eigenvalue and information-gain bound. Kernel-specific corollaries make the result interpretable.

The experiments examine complementary questions: comparison with partition-based contextual methods, sensitivity to arm correlation, and the computational benefit of sparse GP approximations. Repeated runs, error bars, runtime measurements, and a code link improve empirical usefulness.

The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, and it clearly distinguishes its high-probability approximation-regret result from the Bayesian expected-regret result in closely related concurrent work.
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1's information-theoretic derivation is not rigorous for adaptively selected contexts. The selected context vector is not deterministic given only previous selected contexts, and conditional entropy for the data-dependent design requires averaging over histories. The intended inequality appears recoverable using a pathwise log-determinant identity for every realized design, but that argument is not provided. Theorem 1 also squares an upper bound on alpha-regret without establishing that alpha-regret is nonnegative; direct application of Cauchy-Schwarz would avoid this local error.

Necessary: Several claimed applications violate the theoretical assumptions. The model uses an unbounded GP latent function with additive Gaussian observations, whereas probabilistic coverage and the MovieLens experiment require probabilities in [0,1] and use Bernoulli observations. Coverage monotonicity is not guaranteed for un-clipped UCB inputs outside that domain. Similarly, the logarithmic crowdsourcing reward can be undefined under unbounded Gaussian noise. The paper should either narrow its applicability claims or introduce an appropriate link function, clipping rule, and corresponding analysis.

Necessary: The empirical conclusions should be narrowed. MovieLens outcomes are generated from a prescribed sigmoid rather than observed user behavior, and TIM+ with true probabilities is an approximate benchmark, so performance within 0.5% of it does not establish “optimal performance.” Five-run synthetic and semi-synthetic studies support within-experiment comparisons but not the broad claim of vastly outperforming the state of the art.

Necessary: The sparse variant has no confidence or regret guarantee, uses randomly chosen inducing points, and departs materially from the exact posterior analyzed in the theorem. Its heuristic status and precise implementation should be stated more prominently, without suggesting that the main guarantee transfers to it.

Necessary: Reproducibility and notation inconsistencies should be corrected: Simulation I alternates between 250 and 300 rounds; its method description lists 10, 20, and 50 inducing points although results also use 100; the displayed squared-exponential kernel appears to omit the squared distance; and the posterior equations assume zero prior mean after allowing a general mean.

Optional: The evaluation would be stronger with confidence intervals or paired tests, sensitivity to kernel and noise misspecification, scaling studies in K and the number of available arms, matched hyperparameter tuning, and additional relevant baselines. The theory would also benefit from explicitly noting lambda-star is at most K under the normalized kernel and clarifying all K-dependence in the kernel-specific rates.

strengths: The paper studies a well-motivated combination of contextual bandits, combinatorial actions, semi-bandit feedback, and changing arm availability. This has an identifiable audience among bandit and Bayesian-optimization researchers.

O'CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple and modular: GP confidence bounds feed an approximate combinatorial oracle. The batch-covariance argument and the attempt to express regret using arrival-constrained information gain are potentially useful.

The high-level proof strategy is sensible: establish simultaneous GP confidence intervals, use optimism and reward Lipschitzness to control instantaneous regret, and relate accumulated posterior variance to information gain.

The experiments examine several relevant dimensions, including sparse-GP computation, varying outcome correlation, and combinatorial recommendation. They expose the severe computational cost of the exact GP method and suggest a useful accuracy-runtime tradeoff.

The manuscript is generally organized and readable, with pseudocode, an explicit appendix, and legible figures. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-z95zw7p4/call-a33eb445fa094fecb0c19a491fe216bf/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Necessary: The central information-gain proof does not correctly handle adaptive action selection. Appendix A claims that a deterministic algorithm makes z_t deterministic given previous selected contexts, although z_t depends on past random observations. Consequently, the conditional-entropy calculation around Eq. 16 omits the expectation induced by the random design. The result may be repairable using a pathwise log-determinant/Schur-complement identity for every realized action sequence, but that argument is not supplied, so Theorem 1 is not convincingly established as written.

Necessary: The Matérn rate in Corollary 1 is inconsistent with both Theorem 1 and Table 1. Combining Theorem 1 with gamma_N = tilde-O(N^{D/(2nu+D)}) gives a dependence of approximately sqrt(lambda*) (KT)^{(D+nu)/(D+2nu)}, whereas the corollary places T^{(D+nu)/(D+2nu)} inside a square root. This materially overstates the rate and must be corrected throughout.

Necessary: Several additional proof details are formally wrong or incomplete. The proof squares an upper bound on alpha-regret without noting that alpha-regret can be negative; the nonpositive case must be handled separately. The posterior formula is also only valid for a zero-mean prior, despite the paper introducing a general mean function.

Necessary: The claimed applications and experiments often fall outside the theoretical model. Probabilistic coverage is monotone and Lipschitz only on a bounded probability domain, while GP samples and UCB indices are unbounded; TIM+ requires valid probabilities, but no clipping or link function is specified. MovieLens uses Bernoulli rather than Gaussian observations and a randomized (alpha,beta)-oracle rather than the deterministic alpha-oracle assumed by the theorem. Simulation I's logarithmic reward can be undefined or negative under Gaussian noise. The paper must either extend the analysis or clearly label these experiments as heuristic and specify the missing transformations.

Necessary: The MovieLens action definition conflicts with the theorem's cardinality parameter. The manuscript calls K=3 because three movies are selected, but defines base arms as movie-user edges and the super arm as all outgoing edges of those movies; its cardinality can therefore scale with the number of users, not three. This affects the regret dependence, feedback model, and computational claims.

Necessary: The evidence does not justify phrases such as 'vastly outperform,' 'realistic,' or 'optimal performance.' Both datasets supply mainly contexts while rewards are generated by hand-crafted functions; only five runs are used; baseline tuning is not studied; and Simulation II conflates increasing dependence with improving GP model specification because the learner retains lengthscale one while the generating lengthscale varies. The MovieLens comparison also omits CC-MAB for an insufficiently explained interface difference. These claims need substantial narrowing or more controlled comparisons with shared oracles, tuned baselines, more seeds, and uncertainty analyses.

Necessary: Reproducibility is weakened by contradictory details: Simulation I uses T=250 but computes a baseline parameter using 300; the sparse configurations initially list 10, 20, and 50 points but results include 100; Simulation II discusses horizon-specific runs while reporting h_T only for T=300; the displayed 'squared exponential' formula lacks a squared norm; and the Poisson arm counts do not explain how the finite known M required by beta_t is chosen.

Optional: The discussion should more candidly emphasize dependence on a known, correctly specified kernel, explain the worst-case lambda*(K) <= K behavior, describe the sparse approximation precisely, and evaluate robustness to kernel and hyperparameter misspecification. These would improve usefulness but are secondary to repairing the correctness and evidence gaps above.

O'CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple, works with approximation oracles, and is accompanied by a high-probability regret analysis. The availability-aware information-gain quantity and treatment of within-round batch covariance are useful technical contributions.

The experiments cover complementary settings and expose the severe computational cost of the exact GP method. The sparse experiments provide practically useful evidence about the accuracy-runtime tradeoff.
The paper is generally well organized, provides pseudocode and complete proofs, and compares its assumptions and regret rates with closely related work.
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1's proof incorrectly says that z_t is deterministic given the preceding selected contexts merely because the policy and oracle are deterministic. An adaptive deterministic policy still chooses z_t using preceding observed outcomes. Consequently, the conditional-entropy calculation is not justified as written. The likely repair is a pathwise block-determinant/Schur-complement argument for every realized design, but that argument must be supplied. Theorem 1 also squares an upper bound on approximation regret without first handling the case where that regret is negative.

Necessary: Several advertised applications violate the theoretical observation model. Probabilistic coverage requires f(x) in [0,1] and Bernoulli outcomes, whereas the analysis assumes an unconstrained GP and additive Gaussian noise; un-clipped UCB indices may also fall outside the oracle's valid probability domain. In Simulation III, K=3 counts selected movies even though the theoretical K counts selected base arms and the stated super arm contains many movie-user edges. The theoretical applicability claims must be restricted or the model and analysis extended.

Necessary: The empirical language is too strong. The MovieLens and Foursquare experiments use constructed response functions rather than observed online outcomes, only five repetitions are reported, and comparison is largely against two older discretization-based UCB methods. The inducing-point counts are also inconsistent between the setup and results. These details are needed for reproducibility and for interpreting the stated complexity.

Necessary: Corollary 1 should justify its dependence on K. Substituting N<=KT into standard Matérn information-gain bounds introduces additional polynomial K dependence unless K is explicitly treated as an asymptotic constant. The posterior equations should likewise either assume a zero prior mean or include the missing mean corrections.

Optional: More informative evaluation would include sensitivity to kernel misspecification and hyperparameter selection, stronger GP/batch-bandit baselines, uncertainty intervals for pairwise performance differences, and empirical reporting of the eigenvalue quantity appearing in the bound. strengths: The paper addresses a useful, clearly motivated combination of contextual, combinatorial, and changing-action-set bandits. The oracle-based formulation and GP-UCB algorithm are accessible to an identifiable bandit/GP audience. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-f14qcuup/call-9a5e77ea244f49cd8d858b15bc4ff582/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The information-gain analysis appropriately recognizes that semi-bandit observations arrive in batches. The resulting dependence on information gain, action size, and within-batch posterior covariance is informative, and the kernel-specific corollaries make the result interpretable.

The sparse variant addresses a genuine computational limitation of exact GP inference. The experiments examine reward, regret, runtime, and varying correlation, thereby conveying the practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff.

The manuscript is generally well organized, provides pseudocode and an appendix, relates the setting to prior contextual combinatorial bandits, and discusses concrete applications rather than presenting the theory in isolation.
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1 is not proved correctly for adaptively selected actions. A deterministic policy still produces random actions through its random feedback, so z_t is not determined by z_[t-1]; the entropy equalities also omit the expectation over adaptive histories and incorrectly treat the selected noise as unconditioned. The result appears repairable using a pathwise log-determinant factorization for every realized feasible action sequence, followed by the maximum-information-gain bound, but that argument is absent. In addition, the transition from (22) to squared regret is invalid because alpha-regret need not be nonnegative; Cauchy-Schwarz should instead be applied directly to the nonnegative upper bound.

Necessary: Several applications and experiments fall outside the stated model. Bernoulli MovieLens/coverage observations violate the Gaussian-noise assumption, an untransformed GP cannot represent probabilities almost surely, the additive synthetic reward can be negative despite the nonnegative-reward assumption, and the Gaussian noise in Simulation I gives positive probability that its logarithm is undefined. Probabilistic coverage also selects all edges incident to K chosen nodes, so its number of selected base arms is generally much larger than K. These cases require an extended theory or explicit labeling as heuristic, out-of-model demonstrations.

Necessary for the empirical claim: Simulation II keeps the learner's RBF lengthscale at 1 while varying the data-generating lengthscale. Improved performance at larger lengthscales therefore conflates stronger dependence with decreasing kernel misspecification. Matched or tuned kernels are needed to isolate dependency exploitation; otherwise the broad claims that the methods exploit correlation and “vastly” outperform alternatives should be narrowed.

Necessary: Near-equality to a randomized approximate TIM+ benchmark does not establish the claimed “optimal performance” in Simulation III. The setting is semi-synthetic, with outcomes generated from a handcrafted sigmoid rather than observed MovieLens behavior. The conclusion should be stated as near-benchmark performance, and the sparse method should not inherit the exact method's theoretical guarantees implicitly.

Reporting needs correction: the general-prior posterior-mean formula is written only for a zero-mean GP; the sparse construction is ambiguous between data subsampling and variational inducing-point inference; its stated complexity does not clearly follow from the description; and there are inconsistencies involving 250 versus 300 rounds and three versus four inducing-point configurations. The RBF formula appears to omit the squared distance, while the Matérn row of Table 1 and the corollary disagree and the displayed rate suppresses additional polynomial dependence on K when K is not fixed.

Optional: Stronger evidence would include more than five repetitions, confidence intervals, sensitivity to kernel/noise misspecification and oracle randomness, longer-horizon memory/runtime measurements, and comparisons with scalable kernelized or neural contextual-bandit baselines. These would improve scope but are not required for the narrower theoretical contribution.

This should interest researchers working on structured bandits, Gaussian processes, and online allocation.
O’CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple, compatible with approximation oracles, and exploits correlations between contexts without discretizing the context space.

The principal high-probability regret result captures the batch nature of semi-bandit feedback through posterior covariance eigenvalues and an availability-aware information-gain quantity. The kernel-specific consequences make the result interpretable.

The experiments examine complementary questions: performance on semi-synthetic crowdsourcing data, sensitivity to arm dependence, sparse-GP efficiency, and probabilistic coverage using MovieLens structure. Runtime measurements and error bands are useful additions.

weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1’s proof incorrectly argues that a deterministic oracle makes the selected batch z_t deterministic given previous selected contexts. Actions depend on past noisy observations. Consequently, the conditional-entropy calculation omits conditioning or expectations and treats an adaptive information gain as though the sequence were fixed. The result appears repairable by fixing each realized feasible action sequence and applying the block log-determinant identity pathwise, but that argument must be supplied. Theorem 1 should also handle potentially negative α-regret before squaring inequality (22).

Necessary: SO’CLOK-UCB is underspecified. The statement that it uses only a subset of past observations is not equivalent to the cited variational inducing-point method, which ordinarily retains all observations. The paper should specify whether observations are discarded, how inducing points are resampled or optimized, the variational objective and update schedule, and how the stated complexity follows. It should also emphasize that the regret theorem covers only the exact-GP algorithm.

Necessary: several experiments depart from the theoretical model—MovieLens uses Bernoulli observations, a handcrafted non-GP mean function, and a randomized (α,β)-oracle; Gaussian outcomes make the logarithmic reward in Simulation I undefined with nonzero probability; and Simulation II permits negative rewards despite the assumed nonnegative reward. These are reasonable robustness experiments only if the mismatch and absence of corresponding guarantees are stated explicitly.

Necessary: the strongest empirical claims are too broad. Five runs in tailored environments support qualitative trends but not general “state-of-the-art” superiority. In Simulation III, matching a randomized approximate-oracle benchmark does not establish “optimal performance,” and MovieLens supplies contexts while outcomes remain synthetic. These claims should be narrowed, or supported with stronger uncertainty analysis and broader baselines.

Optional: resolve reproducibility and presentation inconsistencies, including 250 versus 300 rounds in Simulation I, the apparently missing squared norm in the stated RBF kernel, unclear learner lengthscales in Simulation II, and the interpretation of standard-deviation bands. Clarifying whether changing context sets are fixed/oblivious or may adapt to prior feedback would also sharpen the theorem’s scope.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated setting combining contextual, combinatorial, and changing-action-set bandits. The proposed oracle-based GP-UCB algorithm is simple, and the intended audience can readily understand and use the main idea. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-j1yg17jl/call-3f086effd4474856ae5b9c2f6d14f78f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The main theorem gives a meaningful high-probability approximation-regret bound that accounts for batched semi-bandit feedback through posterior covariance eigenvalues and an availability-aware information-gain quantity. The confidence and oracle-based instantaneous-regret arguments are largely clear and self-contained.

The kernel-specific corollaries help interpret the abstract information-gain result and compare it with earlier discretization-based approaches without relying on a state-of-the-art-performance claim for publication merit.

The experiments cover accuracy, dependence strength, and computational cost; they include established baselines, repeated runs with variability, and a useful demonstration of the sparse-GP accuracy/runtime tradeoff.
The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly identifies an interested audience in GP bandits and contextual combinatorial optimization.
weaknesses: Necessary: The proof of Lemma 1 treats adaptively selected contexts as though they formed a fixed Gaussian design. A deterministic oracle does not make the next context deterministic from previous selected contexts alone, because selection depends on observed outcomes; consequently, the unconditional entropy identities in equations (16)–(21), particularly H(r(z_[T])|f(z_[T])) as a sum of independent noise entropies, are not justified as written. The likely repair is a conditional-information argument including the complete history and selected locations, or a pathwise Schur-complement/log-determinant proof. The theorem appears salvageable, but the current proof has a real gap. The later squaring of potentially signed approximation regret should likewise handle the negative-regret case explicitly.

Necessary: Several experiments do not instantiate the stated theoretical model. The MovieLens experiment uses Bernoulli observations despite the Gaussian-noise posterior analysis, while an unconstrained GP does not ensure valid probabilities. Simulation I applies a logarithm to Gaussian-noisy sums, which have nonzero probability of leaving the logarithm's domain, and Simulation II permits negative rewards despite the nonnegative-reward assumption. These results should be clearly labeled as heuristic misspecified-model tests, or the models and claims should be revised accordingly.

Necessary: Some empirical conclusions are broader than the evidence. MovieLens supplies features and graph structure, but outcomes are generated from a hand-designed sigmoid, so this is semi-synthetic rather than evidence on real recommendation outcomes. The near-one ratio is relative to a benchmark using the same approximate oracle, not the global optimum. Claims such as “optimal performance,” “vastly outperform,” and suitability for online use should therefore be narrowed; the latter is especially questionable when reported sparse updates still take minutes per round.

Necessary: Experimental reporting contains reproducibility and fairness inconsistencies: Simulation I uses 250 rounds but configures CC-MAB using 300; the sparse setup initially lists 10, 20, and 50 inducing points although results include 100; AOM-MC and CC-MAB are used inconsistently; and the squared-exponential kernel formula omits the squared distance. Baseline tuning and sparse-GP fitting details are also insufficiently documented, and only five repetitions are used.

Optional: The paper would benefit from explicitly bounding λ*(K) using k(x,x)≤1, separating the guarantee for exact O’CLOK-UCB from the unproved sparse heuristic, and correcting smaller notation and wording issues such as “Lipschitz continuity of the expected regret” in the conclusion.

strengths: The paper studies a useful and clearly motivated problem: contextual combinatorial semi-bandits with arbitrarily changing arm availability. This should interest researchers in GP bandits and structured online learning.

O’CLOK-UCB is simple, interpretable, and compatible with approximation oracles. The availability-aware information-gain quantity and batch-covariance argument address a real complication introduced by semi-bandit feedback.

The main high-probability approximation-regret bound and its kernel-specific consequences appear broadly consistent with GP-UCB analysis and provide useful theoretical guidance without relying on a finite context space.

The sparse variant addresses the principal computational limitation. Experiments spanning crowdsourcing, controlled dependence variation, and recommendation consistently illustrate the accuracy–runtime tradeoff and the benefit of transferring information across contexts.
The manuscript is generally well organized, provides concrete applications, includes proofs and implementation details, and communicates its main ideas clearly enough to be useful.
weaknesses: Necessary: Repair several local gaps in the theoretical presentation. In Lemma 1, the selected context z_t is not deterministic given previous selected contexts; it depends on previous noisy observations. The result can likely be established pathwise using the GP log-determinant identity for each realized design, but the current entropy argument does not say this correctly. Theorem 1 also improperly squares an inequality although approximation regret need not be nonnegative; Cauchy–Schwarz should instead be applied directly to its positive upper bound. Equation (1) is only valid for a zero-mean prior, contrary to the preceding general-mean definition.

Necessary: Clearly delimit where the guarantees apply. The theory assumes Gaussian observations, a GP-sampled real-valued outcome function, and a deterministic approximation oracle, whereas the MovieLens experiment uses Bernoulli observations and randomized TIM+, and the sparse method has no stated guarantee. Probabilistic-coverage rewards also require estimates in [0,1], but the UCBs are not clipped. Either extend the analysis or explicitly present these cases as heuristic empirical extensions.

Necessary: Narrow some empirical conclusions. MovieLens supplies real features but the watching probabilities are synthetically generated; closeness to a TIM+ approximate benchmark does not establish “optimal performance”; and comparison with two partition-based methods over five runs is insufficient to claim broad or state-of-the-art superiority. The demonstrated claim is strong performance in the reported simulations.

Necessary: Reconcile reporting inconsistencies: Simulation I uses T=250 but tunes CC-MAB using 300; the sparse configuration initially lists 10, 20, and 50 inducing points although figures include 100; AOM-MC and CC-MAB naming varies; the displayed RBF formula appears to omit the squared norm; and Table 1’s Matérn dependence disagrees with Corollary 1. In the coverage experiment, K=3 counts selected movies, while theoretical K bounds the number of selected base-arm edges.

Optional: Strengthen the empirical study with more repetitions or uncertainty for mean differences, absolute as well as normalized rewards, sensitivity to kernel and noise misspecification, and a comparison to another GP combinatorial-bandit method where implementations permit.

Optional: Give a more reproducible account of sparse-GP fitting and inducing-point resampling, and refine the complexity analysis to include prediction over M available arms and any hyperparameter-optimization costs.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a well-motivated intersection of contextual, combinatorial, and changing-action-set bandits, with an identifiable audience. The problem formulation and oracle-based algorithm are generally clear. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-jm44aksj/call-4de70fd8c98a466b9f30e6d99dd494b0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The availability-aware maximum information gain is useful, and the batch covariance argument captures a genuine distinction from simply treating the problem as a GP bandit with KT sequential rounds.

O'CLOK-UCB is simple and modular: it combines GP confidence bounds with an arbitrary deterministic approximation oracle. The resulting high-probability alpha-regret theorem and kernel-specific rates are potentially useful findings.

The experiments examine complementary questions—reward, dependence exploitation, and computation—and compare against relevant adaptive-discretization baselines. The reported performance differences are often large, and uncertainty across five runs is shown.

The sparse-GP variant addresses the main practical bottleneck of exact GP inference, while the discussion of the closely related 2025 work clearly identifies differences in regret notion and analysis.
weaknesses: Necessary — Lemma 1 is not rigorous for the adaptive design produced by the algorithm. A deterministic oracle does not make z_t deterministic given earlier selected contexts: z_t depends on the random observed outcomes through the posterior mean. Thus the adaptively selected observation vector is not simply jointly Gaussian as used in equations (16)–(18). The likely repair is to formulate the log-determinant identity pathwise for every fixed realized feasible design sequence, exploiting that posterior covariances do not depend on observed values, and then maximize over such sequences. Until this is supplied, the central theorem has a real, although apparently repairable, proof gap.

Necessary — Theorem 1's proof squares R_alpha(T) <= A. Approximation regret can be negative when alpha < 1, so this implication is invalid. Cauchy–Schwarz should instead be applied directly to the nonnegative upper bound A, or the proof should work with the positive part of regret. Also, equation (1) is only correct for a zero-mean GP, despite the paper allowing a general mean function; either assume zero mean or include the standard mean correction.

Necessary — Several claimed applications and experiments do not satisfy the stated model. A GP sample and additive Gaussian observations are unbounded, whereas probabilistic coverage requires outcomes in [0,1] and TIM+ requires valid probabilities; the UCBs are not clipped. The MovieLens experiment uses Bernoulli observations, and the crowdsourcing logarithmic reward is undefined with positive probability under Gaussian noise and is not globally Lipschitz. Moreover, in coverage K=3 counts selected movies, while the theoretical K bounds the number of selected base-arm edges. The paper should either extend the theory with suitable bounded/link-function assumptions or clearly narrow its applicability claims.

Necessary — The empirical language is stronger than the evidence. MovieLens and Foursquare provide contexts, but outcomes are handcrafted or resampled rather than observed recommendation/crowdsourcing outcomes; the MovieLens benchmark is itself approximate. Five runs therefore support an illustrative semi-synthetic comparison, not claims of 'optimal performance,' broadly 'realistic' validation, or decisive state-of-the-art superiority. These claims should be narrowed or supported with stronger real-outcome evaluations and more robust uncertainty reporting.

Necessary — Reproducibility details conflict: Simulation I specifies inducing-point counts 10, 20, and 50 while figures include 100; T=250 is stated but the CC-MAB parameter uses 300; and Simulation II's displayed 'squared exponential' kernel omits the square on the distance. The sparse posterior/update procedure and any probability clipping should also be specified precisely.

Optional — Useful additions would include hyperparameter and inducing-point-selection sensitivity, matched-compute comparisons, numerical result tables, and an ablation showing how the empirical batch covariance or lambda-star varies with K. These would strengthen the paper but are not prerequisites if the central claims are appropriately scoped.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful, well-defined setting combining contextual bandits, combinatorial semi-bandit feedback, and changing arm availability. The oracle-based O'CLOK-UCB algorithm is conceptually simple and relevant to bandit and Gaussian-process researchers.

The principal theoretical contribution is meaningful: the high-probability alpha-regret analysis accounts for batched posterior updates using conditional covariance eigenvalues and an availability-restricted information-gain quantity. Full proofs and kernel-specific corollaries are provided.

The experiments examine complementary aspects: performance on semi-synthetic applications, sensitivity to arm correlation, and the computational tradeoff from sparse GP approximations. Reporting reward, regret, runtime, and variability makes the practical message easy to identify.

The manuscript is generally clear and self-contained, with helpful examples, pseudocode, comparisons, figures, and an appendix. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xhpll1j0/call-5f71a055af7b4da1b2f79ca1178c43cd/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1's entropy argument is not rigorous for adaptively selected contexts. Contrary to the proof, z_t is not determined by previous locations alone; it depends on previous outcomes, and the displayed conditional entropies suppress the corresponding expectation or conditioning on selected locations. The desired result appears recoverable pathwise through the log-determinant identity for every realized design, but this correction should be written explicitly. The proof should also state a zero-mean GP or use the proper nonzero-mean posterior formula, and handle the possibility of negative alpha-regret before squaring it.

Necessary: Several advertised applications fall outside the theoretical assumptions. GP means and UCB indices are real-valued, whereas probabilistic coverage requires values in [0,1] and its reward is not globally monotone under unrestricted indices. The MovieLens experiment additionally uses Bernoulli feedback and a randomized approximate oracle. The paper should either supply clipping/link-function analysis or clearly limit these examples to empirical robustness outside the theorem.

Necessary: The empirical language is too broad. The MovieLens outcomes are generated from a chosen sigmoid rather than observed user behavior, its benchmark is itself approximate, and only five repetitions are used; being within 0.5% of that benchmark does not establish "optimal performance." Claims of realistic, state-of-the-art, or vast superiority should be restricted to the tested configurations.

Necessary: The sparse method is insufficiently specified and internally inconsistent: retaining only s observations is different from the Titsias variational inducing-point approximation and implies different complexity. Other discrepancies include omitting the 100-point configuration from one method description, using T=250 versus T=300 in Simulation I, writing a squared-exponential kernel without a squared distance, and reusing K for movies although the theoretical super arm consists of many movie-user edges.

Optional: Stronger evidence would include more repetitions and confidence intervals, numerical result tables, baseline and kernel hyperparameter sensitivity, and ablations of inducing-point selection. It would also help to state lambda*(K) <= K and discuss why stronger within-batch correlation can worsen this factor even though correlation improves empirical generalization.

strengths: The changing-action-set contextual combinatorial bandit problem is well motivated and relevant to researchers in GP bandits and combinatorial semi-bandits.
O’CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple and modular, combining per-arm GP confidence bounds with a deterministic approximation oracle.

The high-probability alpha-regret result has useful, interpretable dependence on arrival-restricted information gain and within-batch posterior correlation. The treatment of batched semi-bandit feedback is potentially valuable.
The sparse variant addresses an important computational limitation, and the experiments examine accuracy, runtime, inducing-point count, and varying outcome dependence across several settings.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly, provides illustrative applications, and communicates the main algorithm and theoretical intuition accessibly.
weaknesses: Necessary: The proof of Lemma 1 mishandles adaptively selected contexts. The selected action at round t is not determined by previous locations alone, and the adaptively selected values are not unconditionally a fixed-design Gaussian vector as assumed in equations (16)–(18). The variance bound appears recoverable through a pathwise log-determinant argument conditional on each realized design, but that argument is not supplied.

Necessary: Several smaller gaps in the theorem presentation should be repaired: the posterior formula assumes a zero prior mean despite introducing a general mean; the confidence argument requires fixed exogenous arrival sets and a known finite bound M; and squaring the alpha-regret upper bound is unjustified without separately handling potentially negative alpha-regret.

Necessary: Some advertised applications fall outside the formal model. A nondegenerate GP-valued function cannot directly be an activation probability in [0,1]; Simulation III uses Bernoulli observations and a randomized approximate oracle rather than Gaussian noise and a deterministic oracle; and the logarithmic reward in Simulation I is not guaranteed to be defined or nonnegative under unbounded Gaussian noise. These cases should be explicitly presented as heuristic out-of-model evaluations or supported by an extended analysis.

Necessary: The evidence supports superiority in the tested configurations, but not the broad claims of “vastly” outperforming prior methods in realistic settings or attaining optimal performance. There are only five repetitions, the outcomes are synthetic or semi-synthetic, and the MovieLens benchmark itself uses an approximate oracle. These claims should be narrowed.

Necessary: Reproducibility and consistency need improvement. The sparse method is described both as retaining only a data subset and as variational inducing-point inference; important likelihood and kernel details are omitted; and there are inconsistencies including 250 versus 300 rounds, omission of the 100-point configuration from one list, an apparent missing squared norm in the RBF formula, and incompatible Matérn bounds between Table 1 and Corollary 1.

Optional improvement: More repetitions, kernel-misspecification and inducing-point-selection sensitivity analyses, and additional appropriate baselines would make the empirical conclusions more informative, but state-of-the-art performance is not required for acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript clearly formulates a useful setting combining changing arm availability, contextual generalization, combinatorial actions, and semi-bandit feedback; O’CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple and relevant to bandit and Bayesian-optimization researchers. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-slycx052/call-b5674c6613ac44b8bf6a24a39b2605b0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The main analytical route is sensible: simultaneous feedback is handled through batch posterior covariance, an eigenvalue/information-gain bound, and a Lipschitz reduction from arm confidence widths to approximation regret. The resulting high-probability, kernel-dependent rates are informative.

The experiments cover smoothness dependence, sparse-GP computational tradeoffs, and two dataset-derived scenarios. They demonstrate substantial gains over partition-based baselines in the particular smooth settings tested and include a public code link.
The paper is generally well organized and explains its assumptions, algorithm, comparison-oracle framework, and relationship to closely related work clearly enough for the intended audience.
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1 incorrectly states that the adaptively selected context vector z_t is deterministic given previous selected contexts; it also depends on previous noisy observations. The proof applies fixed-design mutual-information identities without properly conditioning on the adaptive design. A pathwise log-determinant proof for every realized context sequence, or a rigorous conditional-information formulation including the selected locations, is needed. Separately, the proof squares R_alpha(T) after only establishing R_alpha(T) <= A, although approximation regret can be negative; Cauchy–Schwarz should instead be applied directly. Both issues appear locally repairable, but the present proof is not fully valid.

Necessary: several advertised applications and experiments fall outside the formal model. A nondegenerate GP and its UCBs are unbounded, whereas probabilistic maximum coverage requires means and oracle inputs in [0,1]; the MovieLens experiment uses Bernoulli rather than Gaussian observation noise; and the crowdsourcing logarithmic reward can be undefined with unbounded Gaussian noise. The authors should add and analyze an appropriate link or clipping construction, or explicitly narrow the theory-to-application claims.

Necessary: SO’CLOK-UCB is insufficiently specified. The description alternates between a variational inducing-point approximation and simply retaining a subset of observations, and it provides neither pseudocode nor confidence/regret guarantees. It should be presented explicitly as an empirical heuristic unless its construction and guarantees are supplied.

Necessary: the experiments justify performance only in the reported configurations, not the abstract’s broad claim of vastly outperforming prior state of the art in realistic setups. MovieLens supplies contexts, but outcomes are generated by a synthetic sigmoid; the TIM+ benchmark is itself approximate, so proximity to it does not establish optimality. Five runs, no tuning protocol, and little kernel/noise sensitivity analysis further limit the conclusion. Narrower claims would suffice, or broader evidence is needed.

Necessary editorial corrections include the 250-versus-300-round inconsistency in Simulation I, omission of the reported 100-inducing-point condition from the algorithm specification, inconsistent AOM-MC/CC-MAB naming, a squared-exponential formula apparently missing the squared distance, and a Matérn rate in Table 1 inconsistent with Corollary 1. Equation 1 also assumes a zero prior mean despite the earlier general-mean formulation.

Optional: stronger evaluation would include compute-matched GP or independent-arm baselines, confidence intervals or seed-level results, tuned baselines, inducing-point selection ablations, kernel misspecification tests, and an explicit worst-case substitution lambda-star(K) <= K to make the regret dependence easier to interpret.

strengths: The problem—contextual combinatorial semi-bandits with changing arm availability—is clearly motivated, formally specified, and relevant to researchers studying structured bandits and Gaussian-process optimization.

O’CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple, and the arrival-aware information-gain quantity plus the within-round covariance argument provide a useful route to a high-probability approximation-regret bound. The main theorem appears repairable despite the proof issue below.

The experiments cover complementary settings, compare against relevant discretization-based methods, report runtime and sparse-GP tradeoffs, average five repetitions with error bars, and provide code. The figures substantiate the narrower claim that GP sharing helps substantially in these particular smooth environments.

The exposition, algorithm, assumptions, and relationship to closely related work are generally understandable; the paper also distinguishes its high-probability approximation-regret result from the Bayesian-regret result for the same setting. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1rf7g8m7/call-dff827d257b74acfac710ea2ddb0af3b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1’s proof mishandles adaptive selection. A deterministic policy does not make z_t deterministic given earlier locations; z_t depends on earlier noisy outcomes. Consequently, the conditional-entropy expressions require conditioning and expectations not shown in equations (16)–(18). The lemma likely can be repaired pathwise using block-determinant/Schur-complement identities for every realized sequence, but the current proof does not establish it. Theorem 1 also squares equation (22) without first handling potentially negative approximation regret.

Necessary: Corollary 1 is not an immediate substitution with the displayed K-dependence. Since Matérn information gain at KT observations scales polynomially in KT, Theorem 1 yields approximately sqrt(lambda-star+sigma-squared) times (KT)^((D+nu)/(D+2nu)), rather than sqrt(lambda-star times K) times T^((D+nu)/(D+2nu)), unless K is explicitly treated as a fixed hidden constant. The abstract and corollary also drop the sigma-squared term without an assumption lower-bounding lambda-star.

Necessary: Several applications and experiments fall outside the proved model without sufficient qualification. MovieLens and probabilistic coverage use Bernoulli observations, whereas the confidence proof assumes Gaussian noise; coverage probabilities also require clipping UCBs to [0,1]. Simulation II permits negative Gaussian rewards despite the stated nonnegativity assumption. In Simulation I, Gaussian noise gives log(1+sum r_i) a nonzero probability of being undefined, and its expectation is not log(1+sum f_i). The setups or claims of theoretical applicability must be corrected.

Necessary claim narrowing or additional evidence: “vastly outperform,” “state-of-the-art,” “real-world,” and “optimal performance” are too broad. The dataset-based outcomes are largely synthetic, Simulation II favors the GP model class, MovieLens uses an approximate benchmark, only five runs are reported, and no other GP combinatorial method is evaluated. The plots support superiority only over the tested baselines in the specified simulations.

Optional: Clarify the exact sparse-GP construction and complexity; reconcile the stated inducing-point sets with the 100-point results; correct the 250-versus-300 horizon inconsistency, the missing squared norm in the squared-exponential kernel, the AOM-MC/CC-MAB naming inconsistency, and the nonzero-prior-mean posterior formula.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-defined, practically relevant intersection of contextual, combinatorial, and changing-action-set bandits, with an identifiable audience in bandit theory and Gaussian-process optimization.

O’CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple and accommodates arbitrary exogenous availability patterns without discretizing the context space. Its use of approximation oracles also covers a useful class of combinatorial problems.

The batch information-gain argument is a meaningful technical contribution. Subject to the proof clarification below, it yields informative high-probability alpha-regret bounds and kernel-specific sublinear rates.

The experiments cover synthetic smoothness variation, two semi-synthetic applications, and computational tradeoffs. Reporting runtime and sparse-GP variants is particularly useful, and the results consistently illustrate the benefit of transferring information between similar contexts.
The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, with helpful application examples, an algorithm diagram, comparisons to related settings, and complete proofs.
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1 is not rigorous as written for adaptively selected actions. A deterministic algorithm does not make z_t deterministic given previous selected contexts; z_t depends on past observed outcomes. Correspondingly, conditional entropy should include an expectation when the design and posterior covariance are history-dependent, whereas equations 16–21 treat realized quantities as deterministic. The likely repair is a pathwise log-determinant identity for every realized context sequence, followed by the maximum-information-gain bound, but this must be stated and proved carefully.

Necessary: several smaller theoretical details should be corrected. Equation 1 silently assumes a zero prior mean although the formulation permits arbitrary mu; squaring the regret bound is invalid without separately handling potentially negative alpha-regret; and the theorem should explicitly state whether availability sets are fixed ex ante or merely predictable.

Necessary for the application claims: probabilistic maximum coverage requires means in [0,1], while a nondegenerate Gaussian process and the unclipped UCB indices are not confined to this interval, where the claimed monotonicity may fail. The MovieLens experiment additionally uses Bernoulli observations and a randomized (alpha,beta)-oracle, while the theory assumes Gaussian noise and a deterministic alpha-oracle. The sparse posterior also has no confidence or regret guarantee. These experiments can remain useful robustness demonstrations, but their relationship to the theorem must be delimited accurately or the model and analysis extended.

Necessary: claims such as “vastly outperform,” “realistic,” “online,” and “optimal performance” are broader than the evidence. The real-data experiments use handcrafted response functions, only five repetitions are reported, the MovieLens benchmark is itself an approximate randomized oracle, and sparse inference still takes hundreds of seconds per late round. These claims should be narrowed; stronger evidence would otherwise require additional baselines, uncertainty analysis, and genuinely logged outcomes.

Necessary for reproducibility: resolve the 250-versus-300-round inconsistency in Simulation I, include the plotted 100-inducing-point condition in the stated configuration, correct or explain the missing squared norm in the purported squared-exponential kernel, and document GP noise settings, hyperparameter fitting, sparse optimization, inducing-point resampling, and timing methodology. The clipped Figure 7 caption should also be repaired.

Optional: comparisons with recent combinatorial GP-bandit methods, sensitivity studies for kernel misspecification and inducing-point selection, more repetitions, and an explicit discussion of lambda*(K) (including the generic lambda*(K) <= K bound) would make the empirical and theoretical lessons substantially easier to interpret.

The main algorithm is conceptually simple, works with approximation oracles, and avoids discretizing the context space. The availability-aware information-gain quantity and batch covariance argument provide a useful route to high-probability approximation-regret bounds.

The distinction from closely related work is meaningful: the paper targets high-probability α-approximation regret rather than only Bayesian expected regret, while handling semi-bandit feedback and changing feasible sets.

The experiments examine runtime, varying arm dependence, and a nontrivial coverage objective. They consistently illustrate the practical value of sharing information through a GP and motivate the sparse variant. The manuscript is generally organized and readable, and code is referenced.
weaknesses: Necessary: the proof of Lemma 1 mishandles adaptive selection as written. A deterministic algorithm does not make z_t deterministic given earlier selected contexts; it depends on earlier outcomes. Consequently, the entropy calculation omits an expectation and does not directly yield the stated pathwise inequality. The result appears repairable by fixing each realized design and using the log-determinant/Schur-complement identity pathwise, followed by maximization over feasible designs, but that argument must replace the current one for Theorem 1 to be formally supported.

Necessary: several experiments fall outside the theorem's assumptions and must be labeled explicitly as robustness demonstrations. Simulation III uses Bernoulli observations and a randomized (α,β)-oracle rather than Gaussian noise and a deterministic α-oracle. In Simulation I, U(r)=log(1+sum r_i) is not always real-valued or nonnegative under Gaussian noise. The reward should be modified or the assumptions and claims narrowed.

Necessary: important protocol inconsistencies impede exact interpretation and reproduction. Simulation I uses T=250 but configures CC-MAB using 300 rounds; the text lists three sparse configurations while figures include four; and Simulation II calls exp(-||x-x'||/(2l²)) a squared-exponential kernel, which normally requires a squared distance. These should be reconciled with the implementation.

Necessary: the empirical language is stronger than the evidence. The MovieLens outcomes are synthetically generated from a handcrafted one-dimensional function, the benchmark uses the same approximate oracle rather than the true optimum, and results use only five repetitions. Claims of a realistic setup, optimal performance, and vast superiority should either be narrowed to these particular semi-synthetic settings or supported with broader experiments and stronger uncertainty reporting.

Necessary clarification: the Matérn corollary suppresses additional K-dependence arising from information gain at KT observations unless K is explicitly treated as fixed, and Table 1 is inconsistent with the corollary about the dependence on λ*(K). The asymptotic convention should be stated and the displayed bounds made consistent.

Optional: the paper would be stronger with approximation-error analysis or sensitivity studies for the sparse variant, clearer inducing-point selection details, and comparisons with another GP-based combinatorial method. These additions are desirable but not required for the basic TMLR interest criterion.

strengths: The paper studies a useful and technically nontrivial combination of contextual, combinatorial, and changing-action-set bandits. The model, O’CLOK-UCB algorithm, and intended applications are presented coherently. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-nc96qz2q/call-29abbde6ebb0465c86244bbc52fec7de/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The main theoretical result is meaningful: a high-probability approximation-regret bound connects batch posterior uncertainty to availability-aware information gain. The eigenvalue argument addresses the simultaneous semi-bandit observations and appears salvageable despite presentation gaps.

The experiments cover complementary synthetic, semi-synthetic, and recommendation settings, compare against relevant discretization baselines, and expose the substantial accuracy–runtime tradeoff of exact versus sparse GP inference.

The manuscript is generally readable, provides self-contained proofs of its central statements, and situates the contribution relative to both earlier contextual combinatorial methods and closely related GP-bandit work.
weaknesses: Necessary: The information-gain proof is not rigorous as written for adaptively selected batches. Conditional entropies are replaced by quantities depending on the realized trajectory without the required expectations, while the text incorrectly says the next batch is determined by prior selected contexts rather than prior observations. A pathwise proof that fixes each realized design and applies the log-determinant identity should repair this, but it must be supplied. The proof should also handle potentially negative approximation regret before squaring it.

Necessary: The stated model and examples are inconsistent. The theory assumes additive Gaussian observations and nonnegative rewards, whereas the coverage and MovieLens experiments use Bernoulli outcomes, and the crowdsourcing logarithmic reward applied to unbounded Gaussian observations can be negative or even undefined. The MovieLens experiment also uses a randomized (alpha,beta)-oracle although the theorem requires a deterministic alpha-oracle. These studies should be explicitly labeled as out-of-model stress tests, or the assumptions and analysis should be extended.

Necessary: In probabilistic coverage, base arms are defined as edges, so choosing three movies can select hundreds of edge arms; consequently the manuscript's identification of K=3 with the theorem's maximum super-arm cardinality is incorrect. The claimed theoretical application and K-dependent interpretation must be revised.

Necessary: Several claims exceed the evidence. Five-run experiments with fixed, largely untuned hyperparameters do not establish that the method 'vastly' outperforms the state of the art generally, and attaining 99.5% of an approximate benchmark does not demonstrate optimality. These conclusions should be narrowed. The Matérn corollary should also restore the polynomial K dependence inherited from gamma_{KT}, or explicitly treat K as fixed.

Optional: Reproducibility and empirical confidence would improve with more runs, sensitivity analyses for kernel and baseline hyperparameters, a precise description of sparse-GP training and inducing-point resampling, and correction of reporting inconsistencies such as 250 versus 300 rounds, omission of the 100-inducing-point configuration, and the squared-exponential formula lacking a squared distance.

strengths: The manuscript formulates a coherent, practically motivated problem combining contextual generalization, combinatorial actions, semi-bandit feedback, and changing arm availability. This should interest researchers in Gaussian-process and combinatorial bandits. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-7sq19pkn/call-f96391bcbf8944e88c3e682e785dba69/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

O’CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple and integrates naturally with deterministic approximation oracles. The availability-restricted information-gain quantity and the dependence on within-batch posterior covariance provide useful insight beyond treating the problem as KT sequential GP-bandit rounds.

The confidence-bound and optimism arguments are mostly transparent, and the main regret theorem appears recoverable through a pathwise block log-determinant argument despite formal problems in the presented proof.

The experiments cover complementary questions: performance against discretization-based methods, sensitivity to arm correlation, and the speed-quality tradeoff from sparse GP approximations. The substantial runtime cost of exact inference is reported candidly.

The manuscript is generally well organized, relates the contribution to both earlier contextual combinatorial work and the contemporaneous identical setting of Sandberg et al., and identifies an audience that can use the findings.
weaknesses: Necessary: Lemma 1 mishandles adaptive action selection. The selected contexts z_t are not deterministic given previous contexts; they depend on noisy observations. Consequently, the stated entropy decomposition—especially H(r(z_[T])|f(z_[T])) as a sum of independent noise entropies—is not justified for the random adaptive sequence. The result appears repairable by fixing each realized sequence, applying the block determinant identity pathwise, and then invoking the maximum over feasible sequences, but that argument is absent.

Necessary: Theorem 1 squares an inequality involving alpha-regret, although alpha-regret can be negative; R<=A does not imply R^2<=A^2. The proof should instead bound the nonnegative confidence-width sum before returning to R. Equation 1 also silently assumes a zero prior mean despite introducing a general mean function; either impose zero mean or use the centered GP posterior formula.

Necessary: The Matérn corollary understates dependence on K when K varies. Substituting gamma_KT=O-tilde((KT)^{D/(D+2nu)}) into Theorem 1 gives O-tilde(sqrt(lambda*) (KT)^{(D+nu)/(D+2nu)}), rather than the displayed sqrt(lambda* K) T^{(D+nu)/(D+2nu)}. Alternatively, the result must explicitly be stated only as a T-rate for fixed K.

Necessary: The application and empirical claims need narrowing. The MovieLens study uses synthetically defined logistic probabilities, Bernoulli feedback, and a randomized (alpha,beta)-oracle, all outside the theorem’s GP-sampled function, Gaussian-noise, and deterministic-oracle assumptions. It therefore demonstrates heuristic robustness, not theoretical applicability or “optimal performance.” Likewise, probabilistic coverage requires a bounded/link GP and clipped indices because an ordinary GP and its UCBs are not valid probabilities and the reward is not globally monotone on R.

Necessary: The sparse method is a central practical contribution but lacks sufficiently precise pseudocode, optimization/update details, and any guarantee. Its reported advantage is credible only for the tested configurations; five repetitions and standard-deviation bands provide limited support for broader claims such as “vastly” outperforming prior methods in realistic settings.

Optional: Reproducibility and presentation would improve by resolving the 250-versus-300-round inconsistency, the omitted 100-inducing-point configuration, AOM-MC versus CC-MAB naming, the missing squared norm in the stated RBF kernel, the questionable exclusion of CC-MAB from Simulation III, and the conflation of three selected movies with the theorem’s number of selected base-arm edges. Tuned baselines and kernel/hyperparameter sensitivity would also make the empirical comparison more convincing.

strengths: The paper studies a well-motivated bandit setting combining contexts, combinatorial actions, semi-bandit feedback, and changing arm availability. Researchers working on Gaussian-process and combinatorial bandits should find the formulation and solution useful.

O’CLOK-UCB is conceptually simple and compatible with approximation oracles. The availability-aware information-gain quantity and the block-covariance/eigenvalue argument provide a meaningful way to handle correlated arms selected before batch feedback arrives.

The experiments cover complementary settings: semi-synthetic crowdsourcing, controlled variation of arm correlation, and MovieLens-based probabilistic coverage. They compare reward, regret, and runtime, include variability over five runs, and demonstrate a useful accuracy–cost tradeoff for sparse GP approximations.
The manuscript is generally self-contained and readable, with clear assumptions, pseudocode, application examples, full proofs, kernel-specific rates, and a public code link.
weaknesses: Necessary: The proof of Lemma 1 is not rigorous for adaptive actions. A deterministic oracle does not make z_t deterministic given previous selected contexts; z_t also depends on random past observations. The authors should formulate the information gain conditionally on the adaptive design or replace the entropy argument with a pathwise block-log-determinant identity. Theorem 1 also squares an upper bound on approximation regret even though that regret may be negative; this can be repaired by considering its positive part or applying Cauchy–Schwarz directly.

Necessary: The stated Matérn dependence on K does not follow from Theorem 1 when K varies. Substituting the usual gamma_KT = O-tilde((KT)^{D/(D+2nu)}) gives a factor proportional to (KT)^{(D+nu)/(D+2nu)}, rather than K^{1/2}T^{(D+nu)/(D+2nu)}. The paper should correct the rate or explicitly state that only T-asymptotics with fixed K are claimed. Equation (1) must also include the prior-mean correction or assume a zero-mean GP.

Necessary: Several showcased applications and experiments fall outside the stated model. An unconstrained Gaussian GP does not produce probabilities in [0,1]; probabilistic coverage is monotone only on its probability domain, while UCB inputs can exceed that domain. The MovieLens experiment uses Bernoulli rather than Gaussian observations, and the crowdsourcing logarithmic reward is undefined on part of the Gaussian noise support. The theory or the applicability claims should be narrowed, or transformed/clipped outcomes and suitable confidence bounds should be introduced.

Necessary: The empirical conclusions are too broad. Five-run comparisons against two baselines without tuning sensitivity or statistical tests support performance in these configurations, but not the claims of broadly “vastly” outperforming the state of the art. Likewise, matching an approximate TIM+ benchmark does not establish “optimal performance.” These claims should be stated as configuration-specific empirical findings.

Optional: The sparse variant lacks precise predictive-update equations, a complete description of how randomly resampled inducing points interact with the Titsias approximation, and any regret guarantee. More methodological detail and a clear separation between guarantees for O’CLOK-UCB and empirical evidence for SO’CLOK-UCB would improve usability.

Optional: Reproducibility is weakened by small inconsistencies: Simulation I has 250 rounds while CC-MAB is configured using 300; the listed inducing-point counts omit the plotted 100-point condition; and the displayed “squared-exponential” kernel uses an unsquared norm. These should be corrected.

The intended theoretical contribution is meaningful: a high-probability alpha-approximation regret bound expressed through availability-constrained information gain and batch posterior covariance. Handling semi-bandit batches is a genuine technical issue.

The exposition generally follows a useful progression from assumptions and applications to the algorithm, regret analysis, and experiments. The proof is decomposed into interpretable optimism, instantaneous-regret, and information-gain lemmas.

The experiments attempt to examine complementary questions, including dependence between arms, sparse-GP speedups, runtime, and application-inspired performance; settings and a code link are provided.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central information-gain proof does not correctly handle adaptive selection. Even with a deterministic oracle, each selected set depends on random past observations. The proof nevertheless treats the selected contexts as deterministic, applies Gaussian entropy formulas to the adaptively selected observation vector without the required conditioning or expectations, and then bounds its information by a maximum defined over fixed designs. Consequently, Lemma 1 and the step from (26) to (27) do not establish Theorem 1 as written. A pathwise log-determinant argument for every realized design may repair this, but it is absent from the manuscript.

Necessary: Several advertised applications and experiments violate the theoretical model. A Gaussian-process sample and additive Gaussian noise are unbounded, whereas probabilistic coverage requires probabilities in [0,1] and Simulation III uses Bernoulli outcomes. Coverage is not monotone over all real-valued UCB inputs, and no clipping or link-function analysis is supplied. In Simulation I, log(1+sum r) can be negative or undefined under Gaussian noise and is not globally Lipschitz on the stated domain. The paper must either narrow its applicability claims or provide a compatible bounded/link-function formulation and analysis.

Necessary: The practically important sparse algorithm is not specified precisely enough to reproduce or audit. The text alternates between a Titsias inducing-variable approximation, which normally uses all observations, and simply retaining a random subset of historical observations. It gives no posterior equations, optimization procedure, update pseudocode, or explanation supporting the stated complexity. Most scalability and application results rely on this underspecified method, for which no guarantee is given.

Necessary: The empirical evidence supports only limited comparative claims. There are five runs, little sensitivity or tuning analysis, theoretically prescribed but apparently untuned baseline parameters, and mostly handcrafted outcomes. The MovieLens benchmark itself uses an approximate randomized oracle, so being within 0.5% of it does not establish “optimal performance.” Claims such as “vastly outperform,” “realistic,” and “optimal” should be substantially narrowed.

Necessary: Multiple protocol inconsistencies impede interpretation: Simulation I has 250 rounds but the CC-MAB parameter is derived using 300; the sparse setup initially lists three inducing-point counts although figures include four; and the displayed squared-exponential kernel lacks a squared norm. The learner kernel is also fixed while the data-generating lengthscale varies, without clearly framing this as misspecification.

Necessary but local: Theorem 1's proof squares an upper bound on alpha-regret even though alpha-regret can be negative, which is not logically valid; Cauchy-Schwarz should instead be applied directly to the nonnegative upper-bound expression. The posterior equations also omit the correction required for the nonzero prior mean allowed by the formulation.

Optional: The paper would benefit from showing when its availability-aware information gain is materially tighter than standard worst-case information gain, reporting stronger statistical summaries and baseline tuning, and clearly separating conclusions about exact O'CLOK-UCB from those about the heuristic sparse variant.

strengths: The manuscript studies a useful intersection of contextual, combinatorial, and changing-action-set bandits. GP generalization is particularly well motivated when newly available arms have unseen but related contexts, giving the work an identifiable audience in bandits and Bayesian optimization. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-o9ojhzw5/call-c5c1b3e843d34cd2a978166e0369098c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The theoretical contribution is substantive: O'CLOK-UCB accommodates approximation oracles and batch semi-bandit feedback, introduces an arrival-aware information-gain quantity, and derives a high-probability alpha-regret bound with explicit linear, RBF, and Matern specializations. The covariance-eigenvalue argument captures the within-round dependence that a naive KT-round reduction misses.

The experiments cover complementary questions: performance on semi-synthetic tasks, sensitivity to arm dependence, the accuracy/runtime tradeoff of sparse GPs, and a nontrivial coverage-style recommendation objective. Comparisons against established discretization-based UCB methods, repeated runs, error bars, and the released code all improve the evidentiary value.

The paper is generally well organized and readable. The model, oracle interface, algorithm, applications, and main proof steps are explained in enough detail for the intended audience to understand and potentially use the approach.
weaknesses: Necessary clarification: the proof of Lemma 1 says that the selected context vector z_t is deterministic given earlier selected contexts. A deterministic oracle does not establish this because O'CLOK-UCB's actions depend on earlier noisy outcomes. Consequently, the adaptive entropy calculation is not justified exactly as written. The result appears repairable by fixing each realized action sequence and using the corresponding pathwise log-determinant identity, or by presenting a formally conditioned adaptive-information argument, but this gap should be closed and the availability process should be stated as fixed or oblivious.

Necessary scope correction: the theory assumes Gaussian observations and a deterministic alpha-approximation oracle, whereas the MovieLens experiment uses Bernoulli outcomes and randomized (alpha,beta)-approximate TIM+. Moreover, there K=3 counts selected movies, while a theoretical super arm consists of all selected movie-user edges and can be much larger. This experiment should be clearly labeled as evidence under model misspecification, and the relevant super-arm cardinality and oracle guarantee should not be identified with those in the theorem.

Necessary modeling correction: an unconstrained GP can produce values outside [0,1], including UCB indices above one, so the probabilistic-coverage interpretation and TIM+ inputs are not automatically valid. Likewise, Gaussian noise gives positive probability that log(1+sum r_i) is undefined in Simulation I. A clipping/link-function or bounded-outcome formulation is needed, or the corresponding application claims must be narrowed.

Necessary claim calibration: the experiments support superiority on the tested simulations, but not the broad statements that the method 'vastly' outperforms prior work in realistic settings or achieves 'optimal performance.' MovieLens supplies real covariates but uses a handcrafted synthetic response model, and its benchmark uses the same approximate oracle rather than the true optimum. Reporting closeness to a clairvoyant approximate-oracle benchmark would be accurate.

Optional improvements: specify the sparse-posterior implementation and inducing-point resampling more fully, consider more than five runs and tuned baseline sensitivity, and resolve reproducibility inconsistencies such as 250 versus 300 rounds, omission of the plotted 100-inducing-point configuration from one list, AOM-MC versus CC-MAB naming, and the apparent missing squared norm in the RBF formula.

Optional technical cleanup: either assume a zero GP prior mean or correct the posterior formulas for nonzero mean; define lambda*(K) explicitly as a posterior-covariance quantity that also depends on the realized contexts and horizon; state its simple upper bound; retain the noise contribution when moving from Theorem 1 to the corollaries; and avoid squaring the potentially negative alpha-regret directly in the proof.
